doc.title: Tommy Newsom and Ross Tompkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Early arranging and writing out scales
summary: Tommy imagined orchestrations while delivering papers and drilled scales in his head, which made playing easier.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Right. You anticipated my question and that was when the arranging bug started for you. Was that something that you were interested in from an early age?
Yeah, I think so, yeah. I used to deliver papers and I’d be kind of imagining an orchestration going on.
Yeah, now see I did the same thing but keyboard stuff. Really.

I think you do stuff like that. It’s like, what is it, unforced practice. I had a long bus ride to school. And I had had a teacher that did me the good favor of making me write out all the scales and you know the three minors and the major scales, in all keys. And I would kind of go over them in my mind, or make up combinations, you know like thirds, up and down thirds.
You know yeah, the harmonic minor and different kinds of —
Yeah I had to learn all that too. And if I had to do it right now, I wouldn’t — it’s been so long ago.
Oh I’ll bet it would come right back to you.
To say them? © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
But you know what it does, it did for me anyhow, to write those things out then when I went to play them it was ten times easier. Because I wasn’t fishing for the note.
I wasn’t even having to read them hardly because boy it stuck in my mind.
